commits.pr_title: [ROCm][Perf] Replace torch.topk in DSA candidate block selection
commits.pr_body: ## Summary `select_candidate_blocks` picks the top-k blocks per row with `torch.topk`, which runs a multi-pass radix select (`computeBlockDigitCounts`, `computeBlockwiseWithinKCounts`, `gatherTopK`). That does two things this caller does not need: - **It orders the results.** The only consumer is `_candidate_flags_kernel`, which does `flags[block] = 1`. Nothing downstream reads the ranking or the scores — only the *set* of selected block ids matters. - **It scans the whole padded workspace.** The logits workspace is padded to `max_model_len`, so `nblocks` is `max_model_len / block_size` no matter how short the context is. Past a row's end every block scores `-inf` and can never win a slot, but `torch.topk` has no way to express a per-row extent, so it reads all of it. This PR replaces that select on ROCm with a Triton kernel: - Each score and its index are packed into one order-preserving `int64` key, so `tl.topk` returns both at once and the separate `_store_candidates_kernel` pass disappears. The float bits are sign-transformed so IEEE order becomes unsigned order, and the index rides inverted in the low bits so ties resolve to the smaller index, matching `torch.topk`. - Each row is bounded by its own `end`, which is the part `torch.topk` cannot do. At 4K context in a 256K workspace this skips ~98% of the columns. - Decode rows are `batch * next_n`, only 1–640, which is too few to fill the GPU one program per row. Rows are split across programs and merged, with the split size computed **on device** from each row's live extent — a host-side bound would need a sync, and sizing from the padded width instead measured 6.3x → 2.0x at low concurrency. **The CUDA path is unchanged**; the new kernel is behind `current_platform.is_rocm()`. ## Not a duplicate Checked open PRs touching this area: - **#57858** is the only other open PR touching `candidate_blocks.py`, but it optimizes **prefill consumer-layer scoring** (`candidate_mqa_logits`, scoring only candidate columns). The producer-side block select this PR rewrites is untouched there. The two are complementary. Note #57858 also flips `_store_candidates_kernel`'s NaN handling (`!=` → `>`); the ROCm path here bypasses that kernel entirely, so the behaviors do not collide. - **#48726** (LiteTopk) is the indexer's *token* top-k, a different kernel and stage. - **#50470**, **#46172**, **#56944** touch `rocm_aiter_mla_sparse.py` only (AITER dispatch, indexer optimization, prefill row sharding), not block candidate selection. No open PR optimizes `select_candidate_blocks`. ## Correctness The new path must select the same block *set* as the existing path. Verified against the unchanged path across 27 configurations — contexts 512 to 262144, rows 1 to 640, ragged per-row ends, non-zero `row_ks` starts, `row_repeat` decode grouping, `topk_blocks > nblocks`, and NaN scores: ``` 27 cases, 0 mismatches ``` Two cases this caught during development, both now handled: - `torch.topk` ranks NaN *highest*, and `_block_scores_kernel` can emit NaN during warmup, so keys force NaN above `+inf`. - When `nblocks < topk_blocks` the internal `K_PAD` shrinks below the output width, leaving tail columns unwritten; they are now `-1` filled. ## Tests ``` $ pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_rocm_aiter_candidate_mask.py -q 9 passed, 14 warnings in 4.23s $ pre-commit run --files vllm/model_executor/kernels/attention/dsa/candidate_blocks.py exit=0 (no failures) ``` ## Kernel performance (MI355X) Full `select_candidate_blocks`, CUDA-graph timed, swept over the decode shape space: concurrency 1–128 x spec-decode depth 1–5, `max_model_len=262144`, `block_size=8`, `k=64`. All 120 points are faster. | context | median | range | | --- | --- | --- | | 4096 | 4.16x | 3.97–5.08x | | 16384 | 3.99x | 3.27–4.70x | | 65536 | 2.94x | 1.64–3.15x | Representative points (microseconds): | context | conc | next_n | rows | before | after | speedup | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 4096 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 47.55 | 11.20 | 4.24x | | 4096 | 32 | 1 | 32 | 58.00 | 13.96 | 4.16x | | 4096 | 128 | 5 | 640 | 293.54 | 67.86 | 4.33x | | 16384 | 32 | 1 | 32 | 59.19 | 14.31 | 4.14x | | 16384 | 128 | 5 | 640 | 299.65 | 91.67 | 3.27x | | 65536 | 32 | 1 | 32 | 60.31 | 19.30 | 3.13x | | 65536 | 128 | 5 | 640 | 330.51 | 185.83 | 1.78x | These shapes are TP-independent: the DSA indexer is replicated across ranks (`index_n_heads` is not divided by `tp_size`, unlike the main attention heads), so TP2 and TP4 run identical selections and one sweep covers both. ## Notes The kernel is still well above the bandwidth roofline (~45x at the largest shapes, more at small ones where it is latency-bound on two launches), so there is headroom left. `TILE=512` is a compromise: 1024 would take 65536-context from 2.36x to 2.79x but drop 4096-context from 23.8x to 14.4x. A context-aware tile choice could get both. Benchmarks used uniform context per batch; heavily ragged batches are bounded by their longest row. ## End-to-end serving Measured on MI355X TP4, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, dspark MTP (5 speculative tokens, acceptance pinned at 3.51 so acceptance variance cannot contribute). Both arms are the **same build** differing only by an env toggle on the selection path, run concurrently on separate 4-GPU sets, after a warmup pass over every shape so Triton JIT and graph capture are paid before measurement. snapshot of trace: Before: After: **There is no measurable end-to-end difference, and none should be expected.** Output throughput, ISL 4096 / OSL 128: | concurrency | baseline tok/s | this PR tok/s | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | 259.4 | 257.1 | | 8 | 1287.7 | 1282.4 | | 32 | 1068.9 | 1070.3 | | 128 | 1253.8 | 1254.8 | Repeating a single configuration three times shows run-to-run spread of 1112–1191 tok/s on baseline and 1142–1166 on this branch, with the sign of the difference flipping between repeats. The noise floor is several percent, while the expected effect is about 0.2%: the selection saves roughly 45 us per step against a 14.6 ms inter-token latency. The kernel win is real but it is a sub-1% slice of step time, so it cannot show up above noise in serving throughput. Median ITL, the most stable metric here, is unchanged (14.59-14.64 ms baseline vs 14.61-14.73 ms this branch). This PR should therefore be read as removing a hotspot that is prominent in kernel traces and cutting its cost 2-5x, not as an end-to-end throughput win. ## AI assistance AI assistance was used for this change.

commits.pr_title: [Feature] Add fixed-token prefill scoring
commits.pr_body:
## Summary

This PR adds request-wise fixed-token prefill logprob scoring for OPD / top-k distillation:

- `SamplingParams.prompt_logprob_token_ids`: candidate token IDs to score.
- `SamplingParams.prompt_logprob_start`: absolute first causal prompt row to score.

The result is returned through the existing engine-core and `RequestOutput` paths for the V2 GPU runner.

This is M1 of RFC #56860. Per-position candidate lists (M2) are tracked there.

## Design

For a prompt of length `C` followed by student-generated output tokens, the hidden state at row `i` predicts token `i + 1`. Therefore the first output token is predicted by row `C - 1`. An OPD request sets:

```python
prompt_logprob_token_ids=teacher_topk_union
prompt_logprob_start=C - 1
```

This returns exactly the student probabilities needed for the output suffix. It does not score the earlier context rows. The dedicated result is source-row aligned and contains only requested rows; unlike `prompt_logprobs`, it does not add a leading `None` sentinel.

The candidate IDs are request-wise and fixed across positions, matching M1 of #56860. For each scheduled prefill chunk, the runner converts the absolute start into the chunk-relative row range, runs the lm-head only on that range, and gathers the requested IDs. The worker keeps one `[num_scored_rows, num_ids]` buffer per request, allocated on the first prefill chunk and written in place chunk by chunk, and emits it on the last chunk. Nothing is concatenated, and a request whose start is past the last scorable row emits an empty buffer rather than nothing.

This bounds intermediate memory by the requested suffix and candidate width rather than the full prompt. With `prompt_logprob_start=C-1`, the retained result is proportional to the generated output length. The implementation intentionally keeps the existing chunking and output plumbing instead of adding a new sparse protocol.

### Scoring reuses the sampler's kernel

Scoring calls the existing `compute_token_logprobs()` rather than computing `gather - logsumexp` in the logits' own dtype. That kernel already does exactly this gather: it accumulates max and logsumexp in fp32 and emits only the requested columns, so it materializes no `[tokens, vocab]` tensor either.

The kernel indexed `token_ids` as contiguous rows. It now takes a row stride for `token_ids`, as it already did for `logits`, so the request-wise IDs are passed as a broadcast `[rows, num_ids]` view (stride 0) and are never copied out per row. Existing callers pass contiguous tensors and are unaffected.

This matters numerically. Reducing over a 151936-entry bfloat16 vocabulary loses about 1e-1 of accuracy; against vLLM's own `prompt_logprobs` on the same forward pass, an in-dtype reduction disagreed by up to 7.78e-02. Through the shared kernel the values are bit-identical to `prompt_logprobs` (see Verification).

## Naming

The request-side parameters follow the existing `logprobs` / `prompt_logprobs` prefix convention: `SamplingParams.logprob_token_ids` already exists on main (#43463) and scores caller-supplied token IDs at sampled positions, so `prompt_logprob_token_ids` is its prefill counterpart.

The result is named after that parameter: `RequestOutput.prompt_token_id_logprobs`, a plain `[num_scored_rows, len(prompt_logprob_token_ids)]` float32 array whose columns follow the order the IDs were requested in. The IDs are not echoed back: the caller supplied them, so a container pairing them with the scores would carry nothing the caller does not already have, and nothing between the worker and the output needs them either.

Returning `list[dict[int, float]]` instead would cost ~22 MB of Python objects for a 1000-row, 242-ID request against ~1 MB for the array, and callers doing top-k distillation want the array rather than dicts they have to re-flatten.

## Token-in/token-out HTTP and the Rust frontend

`/inference/v1/generate` takes raw `SamplingParams`, so it accepts both parameters; the non-streaming response returns the scores as `prompt_token_id_logprobs`, a base64 `.npy` float32 array (`np.load(io.BytesIO(base64.b64decode(s)))`), the encoding `routed_experts` already uses on this endpoint. Streaming follows `prompt_logprobs`: the Python frontend omits the field, the Rust frontend rejects the request.

`EngineCoreOutput` is `array_like` on the Python side and decoded positionally by the Rust engine-core client (`Deserialize_tuple`), so the field is appended last there too, kept as the wire ndarray with its aux frame resolved in place; the server writes its float32 bytes straight into the `.npy`. The Rust frontend forwards `prompt_logprob_token_ids` / `prompt_logprob_start` and, since it bypasses `InputProcessor`, checks the candidate count against `max_logprobs` and the ids against the vocabulary, as it does for `logprob_token_ids`. Its `.npy` encoder is byte-identical to `numpy2base64`. OpenAI routes are unchanged.

## Limits

The candidate count is bounded by the existing `max_logprobs` (`--max-logprobs`, default 20), not by a new constant. One logprob per requested ID is returned per scored row, which is exactly the quantity that setting already bounds for `logprobs` and `prompt_logprobs`, and `-1` opens it to the whole vocabulary here too. A distillation workload wanting a few hundred candidates therefore needs the operator to raise `--max-logprobs`, the same opt-in the existing full-vocabulary path requires.

Because the default rejects any realistic candidate set, this is the first error most callers of the parameter will meet, so it names the value to set rather than just the setting:

```
Requested prompt_logprob_token_ids of length 242, which is greater than
max allowed: 20. Set max_logprobs (--max-logprobs) to at least 242.
```

Both spellings appear because `--max-logprobs` is not what a caller using `LLM(...)` sets. The sibling errors in `_validate_logprobs` carry no such hint; the asymmetry is deliberate, and easy to drop if reviewers would rather keep them uniform.

The parameter is implemented for the V2 GPU runner only, so the input processor rejects it with a `VLLMValidationError` naming `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1` when that runner is not in use, rather than letting the V1 runner return `None`. `prompt_logprob_start` without `prompt_logprob_token_ids` is likewise rejected instead of being silently ignored.

`logprob_token_ids` keeps its own `MAX_LOGPROB_TOKEN_IDS = 128` because that number is physical: it is the row width `LogprobTokenIdsState` preallocates. Prompt scoring allocates per request, so it has no such structural bound and does not need a constant of its own.

On the output path the result is owned by `LogprobsProcessor` alongside sample and prompt logprobs, and reached through the same single `update_from_output` call. That also gives it the same `RequestOutputKind.DELTA` handling: like prompt logprobs it is popped, so a streaming request carries it on exactly one output at the end of prefill instead of re-attaching the array to every later delta.

It is kept out of `prompt_logprobs_dict` deliberately: `LogprobsTensors` carries an implicit target-token column and a rank column, neither of which is meaningful for a caller-fixed ID set, and `prompt_logprobs` prepends a `None` sentinel for position 0 that this result must not have. Reusing that container would mean populating two columns with placeholder values and then documenting that they are meaningless.

## Relationship to SGLang

SGLang main uses the same two concepts: request-wise `token_ids_logprob` and an absolute `logprob_start_len`. Its scheduler converts the absolute position to a per-chunk pruned range, and its logits processor applies the lm-head only to suffix hidden states. This V2 implementation follows that lifecycle and offset model while reusing vLLM's existing chunk helper and logprob kernel.

SGLang main does not currently expose a per-position candidate-ID API; this PR therefore does not add one. Per-position candidates are proposed as M2 in #56860.

## Scope / non-goals

This is M1 of #56860. It does not add per-position candidate lists (M2 in #56860), streaming updates, a scoring-only lifecycle, speculative/beam support, multimodal scoring, prefix-cache reads, or an OpenAI protocol field. Those can be evaluated separately if a concrete caller requires them.

This is complementary to open PR #39351 (generative scoring with `max_tokens=0`, which targets next-token scoring) and #49171 (skipping logits for unfinished chunk prefills). This PR scores arbitrary fixed IDs at selected prefill positions. No other open PR adds fixed-ID prefill scoring.

## Verification

All runs used the vLLM nightly container (`0.28.1rc1.dev388+g8a728663c`) on 4x GB200, with this branch's Python layer overlaid on the image's compiled package. Performance runs used a dedicated node with the checkpoint staged in `/dev/shm`.

### Correctness

`Qwen3-0.6B`, 193-token prompt (`193 % 64 == 1`, so the final prefill chunk holds a single token), 10 checks, all passing:

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Chunked prefill (64 tokens/chunk) row count vs unchunked | identical |
| Chunked values vs unchunked | max abs diff `0.00e+00` |
| Values vs vLLM's own `prompt_logprobs=-1`, same request | max abs diff `0.00e+00` |
| Full-vocab `prompt_logprobs=-1` row normalizes | logsumexp over 151936 entries = `+1.24e-07` |
| Row alignment (scan row offsets -2..+2 against HF) | offset 0 median `0.051`; ±1 median `2.43` / `2.43` |
| Result shape / dtype | `(92, 7)` float32 |
| vs HuggingFace `log_softmax` reference | median `5.12e-02` |

The last row needs a control, since vLLM and HuggingFace disagree on this model regardless of this feature. Running vLLM's own `prompt_logprobs` against the same HF reference on the same prompt gives median `4.95e-02`. The residual is the pre-existing vLLM-vs-HF gap (TRTLLM attention, bfloat16), not this path: the two agree to within 3%.

Row alignment is worth calling out separately: a ±1 row shift would still look plausible on a single-number comparison, but scanning offsets shows offset 0 fitting 47x better than its neighbours.

### Preemption

Preemption in the middle of a chunked prefill needs no special handling: the V2 scheduler reports a resumed request as a new one, and the runner drops the worker's state on preemption (`finish_requests` runs before `add_requests`), so the partial buffer is discarded and the re-prefill rebuilds it from the first chunk and emits it once. A resumed request whose prefill had already completed is the case that does need a guard:

A request resumed after preemption re-prefills its prompt plus the tokens it already generated. Those rows are not prompt positions, and its scores were emitted before the preemption, so the accumulator has to skip the resumed prefill — the same condition `compute_prompt_logprobs` already guards with `prompt_lens < prefill_len`. An earlier revision of this PR did not, which is not a silent numerical error: the resumed request emits a result on a step that must produce none, and the engine dies on the scheduler's own invariant.

```
File "vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 2131, in update_from_output
    assert not prompt_token_id_logprobs
AssertionError
```

`test_prompt_logprob_token_ids_with_chunking_and_preemption` is added to `tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs.py`, next to the existing prompt-logprobs preemption test and reusing its setup for forcing chunking and preemption. Verified as a regression test in both directions: it fails with the above assertion against the pre-fix code and passes with the guard in place.

### Performance

`Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507`, TP4, 8192-token context, median of 5 reps, `prompt_logprob_start` set to score the last N rows:

| Scored rows x candidate IDs | median | vs baseline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| baseline (no scoring) | 75.2 ms | — |
| 1000 x 64 | 77.1 ms | +2.0 ms |
| 1000 x 242 | 77.7 ms | +2.6 ms |
| 1000 x 1024 | 80.6 ms | +5.5 ms |
| 4000 x 64 | 80.7 ms | +5.6 ms |
| 4000 x 242 | 81.7 ms | +6.6 ms |
| 4000 x 1024 | 88.9 ms | +13.7 ms |
| `prompt_logprobs=0`, all 8192 rows | 146.2 ms | +71.0 ms |

Row count dominates: at a fixed 64 IDs, going 1000 -> 4000 rows costs +3.6 ms, while at 1000 rows a 16x increase in candidates (64 -> 1024) costs +3.5 ms. In the intended distillation range the feature is roughly 10x cheaper than the existing full-row path while returning far more per row.

Cost grows with `rows x ids`, and at a wide candidate set it crosses over (separate run, baseline 76.6 ms):

| Scored rows x candidate IDs | median | vs baseline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4000 x 1024 | 89.6 ms | +13.0 ms |
| 4000 x 4096 | 108.4 ms | +31.7 ms |
| 4000 x 16384 | 176.0 ms | +99.4 ms |
| `prompt_logprobs=0`, all 8192 rows | 146.1 ms | +69.5 ms |

So 16384 candidates over 4000 rows costs more than scoring every row with `prompt_logprobs=0` — though it returns 16384 candidates per row rather than one target token. The crossover is around 40M `row x id` pairs; beyond that, callers should compare against the full-row path. This is another reason the ceiling is `max_logprobs` rather than a constant of our own: the operator who opens that gate is the one accepting the cost.

### Commands

```bash
# correctness (11 checks) and the two sweeps above
MODEL=/models/Qwen3-0.6B ./_bench/run.sh test_correctness.py
MODEL=/models/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 TP=4 CONTEXT=8192 ./_bench/run.sh test_perf.py

# upstream tests covering the changed kernel and the preemption path
pytest -q tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs.py::test_prompt_logprob_token_ids_with_chunking_and_preemption \
          tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs.py::test_prompt_logprobs_with_chunking_and_preemption
# -> 2 passed in 79.69s   (1 failed against the pre-fix code, as above)

pytest -q tests/v1/engine/test_logprobs_processor.py
# -> 3 passed in 1.12s    (adds the DELTA pop test)

pytest -q tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs.py -k "logprob_token_ids"
# -> 6 passed in 5.22s    (adds the max_logprobs ceiling test, which also
#    pins that the message names the value to raise the setting to)

cargo test -p vllm-engine-core-client
# -> 102 passed, including python_msgpack_fixtures_match_rust_encoding, which
#    round-trips fixtures generated from the current Python definitions
cargo fmt --check   # clean

pre-commit run   # ruff, ruff-format, mypy-3.10, SPDX, forbidden-imports: all pass
```

AI assistance was used for this change. The submitting human has reviewed every changed line and reran the tests above.

## Update 2026-09-17: re-verification after merging main, Rust e2e, audit fixes

Re-run on the merge commit with the `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` container of 2026-09-15 (`0.29.1rc1.dev47+gdc36fcce9`), this branch's Python overlaid, GB200.

- `tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs.py -k prompt_logprob_token_ids`: 3 passed. The chunked-prefill/preemption test now also compares its scores against an unchunked, unpreempted run of the same requests (`rtol=0.1`: batch composition moves bf16 tail logprobs by ~2%, a misaligned row differs by nats). `tests/v1/engine/test_logprobs_processor.py`: passes.
- Correctness script: 10/10 (chunked vs unchunked `0.00e+00`, vs `prompt_logprobs=-1` `0.00e+00`, row-offset scan picks 0).
- Perf (same setup as above, baseline 77.2 ms): 1000×64 +0.9, 1000×242 +1.6, 1000×1024 +3.9, 4000×64 +4.4, 4000×242 +5.6, 4000×1024 +11.3 ms; `prompt_logprobs=0` all rows +73 ms.
- **Cost with the feature off**: every per-step touchpoint mirrors the existing `prompt_logprobs_dict` one beside it (an unconditional worker call that returns on an empty dict, one dict comprehension over an empty dict, one `dict.get` per request in the scheduler, a trailing `None` field that `omit_defaults` drops from the wire). Measured A/B on one GB200, Qwen3-0.6B, 256 requests × 256 greedy decode steps, no scoring params, merge base vs this branch, two alternating rounds: 4.059 / 4.121 ms per step (base) vs 4.138 / 4.094 ms per step (branch); the round-to-round drift (1.5%) is larger than the A/B difference in either direction.
- **Rust frontend e2e** (`VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1`, `vllm-rs` built from this branch, Qwen3-0.6B, chunked prefill at 64 tokens): the same `vllm serve` config brought up with the Python and the Rust frontend agrees on greedy completions, `echo` logprobs (the lm_eval/CI path) and `prompt_logprobs`, and a 32-request concurrent burst matches sequential greedy; 17/17. `cargo test -p vllm-engine-core-client`: 113 passed. The binary has to come from this branch: the Rust client decodes `EngineCoreOutput` positionally with a fixed length, so a `vllm-rs` built before this PR rejects the appended field (`array had incorrect length, expected 17`).

**Audit fixes** (Codex, read-only, on the diff). Two configurations let a prefill skip prompt rows that must be scored, which would have emitted uninitialized rows; one is rejected here, the other is fixed for `prompt_logprobs` too. An explicit `skip_reading_prefix_cache=False` is left to the caller, as it is for `prompt_logprobs`:

1. A KV connector prefix hit: `skip_reading_prefix_cache` gated only the local prefix cache, so a remote hit (NIXL, LMCache, Mooncake, MoRIIO) skipped rows for `prompt_logprobs` as much as for this feature. Split out as #57269, which makes the scheduler discard the hit for such requests; this PR depends on it and no longer carries that change itself.
2. `--kv-sharing-fast-prefill` (Gemma3n) leaves non-sampled rows without the cross-decoder; rejected, as `prompt_logprobs` already is in `AsyncLLM`, but in `InputProcessor` so both engines agree.

Not changed: with `n > 1` every child scores the prompt and, in DELTA mode, each child's first output carries the matrix, exactly as `prompt_logprobs` behaves today.

## Update 2026-09-20: partially scored prefills

A second review found that a prefill can begin past `prompt_logprob_start`, leaving the leading rows of the score buffer unwritten while the buffer is still emitted at its full shape. Two ways in: a caller passing `skip_reading_prefix_cache=False` explicitly (the force-set in `__post_init__` only applies when the flag is left `None`), and a streaming-input session, which extends its prompt in place and keeps its computed tokens, so the next prefill starts mid-prompt with `prefill_len == prompt_len`.

`prompt_logprobs` degrades on the same paths by returning fewer entries. This path was worse: the shape stayed correct and the leading rows carried uninitialized device memory. With the guard removed, the new regression test shows what a caller would have received:

```
array([[ 1.84094184e-40,  0.00000000e+00,  1.85467457e-40],
       [ 0.00000000e+00,  1.87048122e-40,  0.00000000e+00], ...
       [-2.19386425e+01, -2.27218456e+01, -2.54796581e+01]], dtype=float32)
```

The leading rows are denormals rather than log probabilities, and `exp` maps them to ~1.0 — the worst direction for a distillation target.

The worker now drops a request whose first scoring chunk starts past its first scored row (`chunk_start > req.start`), so the caller gets no scores rather than fabricated ones. This covers both entry points without an admission gate, and the condition is exact: a chunk starting before the first scored row still writes every scored row and is emitted as before.

Also in this update: `trace_decode_token_ids` rejects `prompt_logprob_token_ids` as it already rejects `prompt_logprobs`, and the row convention (row i predicts prompt token i+1, last prompt row excluded, result shape) is stated on the parameter and the result instead of only in the tests.

Verification: `tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs.py -k prompt_logprob_token_ids` 4 passed, correctness 10/10 on the same GB200 setup. The new test is a real regression test: with the guard removed it fails with the array above.

## Update 2026-09-21: `/inference/v1/generate`, Python and Rust

Before this update the endpoint accepted the parameters, scored the prompt, and dropped the result: `GenerateResponse` had no field for it, and the Rust frontend silently discarded the parameters. Both frontends now return it (see "Token-in/token-out HTTP and the Rust frontend" above).

commits.pr_body: ## Purpose `ROCmLatentMoERunner` has a column-parallel tail that splits the routed-expert up-projection across ranks and accumulates each rank's shard into its slice of the shared-expert output with `addmm_`, so the shared+routed combine costs no extra kernel. It was gated on `moe_config.tp_size > 1`, which vLLM sets to `1` under expert parallelism, so under `--tensor-parallel-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel` the tail has never run: every rank computed the full 3584 -> 7168 projection and then added the shared output in a separate elementwise kernel. `moe_config.tp_size` describes how the *experts* are split. How many ranks share the hidden dimension is a different question, and its answer is the TP process group world size — which is also the group that `get_tensor_model_parallel_rank()` indexes and that `tensor_model_parallel_all_reduce()` reduces over. This derives the gate and the shard size from that world size instead. `_shard_up_proj_tail` needs no change; it already indexes with the TP rank, which is now consistent with the shard size. The arithmetic is unchanged and holds under EP: the latent is all-reduced before the up-projection so its input is replicated, `shared_output` is still an unreduced TP partial because the dense layers and the shared expert stay at TP=8, and the final all-reduce still fires (`ep_size > 1`). commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Use the correct repository revision for secondary artifact loaders
commits.pr_body:
Bugfix for two regressions introduced in #51446. That PR added revision pins to two secondary-artifact loads, but each used the wrong repository's revision. When a model and its tokenizer are pinned to different revisions, both loads fail.

- **Chat template (`renderers/hf.py`):** loading a chat template from the tokenizer's processor used the model's revision instead of the tokenizer's. Now uses the tokenizer's revision, which falls back to the model revision when unset, so the common case is unchanged.
- **FunAudioChat speech tokenizer (`funaudiochat.py`):** the speech tokenizer is loaded from the model's repository but was pinned to the tokenizer's revision. Now uses the model revision, matching the feature extractor that loads from the same place.

AI assistance was used for this change (GPT-5.6-sol).

commits.pr_title: [Perf][Qwen3.8] Reduce PLE metadata construction overhead
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

PLE metadata construction still synchronizes in mixed speculative batches and builds temporary tensors that its consumers do not need. This reduces per-step builder work while preserving request ordering, accepted-token routing, and persistent CUDA graph buffers.

- Supply `repeat_interleave` with the output size from CPU query offsets, excluding token padding, and use `index_fill_` for request-group labels to avoid scalar-assignment synchronization.
- In pure speculative batches, use request-prefix views instead of uploading indices and gathering state/acceptance tensors. Skip the unused device query-length calculation and identity token maps; request padding remains trailing.
- Let PLE skip generic causal-conv prefill metadata that neither PLE implementation consumes. Other Mamba builders retain the existing default.
- Reuse the builder's prefill query offsets in NVIDIA and AMD PLE consumers.

Related to #55922. This follows the already-merged #55054, which made request-index uploads asynchronous; the changes here remove additional work and mixed-batch synchronization. I checked the tracking issue and its comments, open PRs referencing it, and searches for `PLE metadata`, `short_conv_attn`, and `PleShortConvAttentionMetadataBuilder`. No open PR implements this change. The related CPU backend, quantization, QSA, and standalone PLE state-kernel PRs address different paths.

## Test Plan

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple.py \
  tests/v1/attention/test_mamba_update_block_table.py -q
```

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] Implement get_top_tokens() on the ROCm DeepSeek V4 MTP drafter
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Enabling `speculative_config.use_local_argmax_reduction` with a `deepseek_v4` draft model **fails
engine startup** rather than falling back to the full-vocab path:

```
ValueError: use_local_argmax_reduction is enabled but draft model DeepSeekV4MTP
does not implement get_top_tokens().
```

Both opt-in sites probe the draft model with `hasattr(model, "get_top_tokens")` and raise when it
is missing (`vllm/v1/spec_decode/llm_base_proposer.py:1606`,
`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:387`), and `DeepSeekV4MultiTokenPredictor` implements
only `compute_logits`. So the flag is a trap for every `deepseek_v4` checkpoint: it does not run
slower, it does not start.

`model_type: deepseek_v4` is rewritten to `DeepSeekV4MTPModel` by its own branch in
`SpeculativeConfig.hf_config_override`, which the registry resolves to the per-platform
`DeepSeekV4MTP`, so the generic MTP drafter fix in #56995 does not reach it.

**Fix.** Forward to `LogitsProcessor.get_top_tokens()` from both the predictor and the wrapper in
the ROCm implementation (`amd/mtp.py`), mirroring the `compute_logits` pair already in the file.
The `nvidia` and `xpu` drafters are not changed: this was verified on MI355X only, so they are
left to a follow-up that can be tested on that hardware.

V4 reaches its LM head through `hc_head` over the `(T, hc_mult, D)` residual and then the shared
head's RMSNorm, unlike V3 (`shared_head` alone) and V3.2 (an already-normed hidden state). Running
a different transform returns a *different draft token* instead of failing, so that transform is
factored into `_pre_head()` and shared by `compute_logits` and `get_top_tokens` rather than written
twice.

`use_local_argmax_reduction` defaults to `False` and gates every call site, so the default path is
unchanged.

## Test Plan

Hardware: MI355X (`gfx950`), HIP 7.2.53211, torch 2.11.0. Measurements ran against a substrate
built from upstream `releases/v0.27.1` (the sha the host's build names) plus that build's compiled
extensions; in the region this PR touches, v0.27.1 and `main` differ only in how the shared-head
RMSNorm kernel is re-exported, so the arms transfer. The two arms are one tree differing in exactly
one file (`diff -r`).

1. **Unit tests** (added, ROCm only; the module skips before importing the ROCm drafter elsewhere):
   `pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dsv4_mtp_local_argmax.py`, asserting that the token
   `get_top_tokens` selects carries the row maximum of the full-vocab logits. Re-run on a v0.30.0
   substrate after rebasing onto current `main`.
2. **Falsifiability**: the same tests run against the merge base, and against two deliberately
   wrong implementations — the shared-head RMSNorm dropped, and `hc_head` dropped.
3. **Micro, TP=2**: both arms as methods on the same predictor over a real TP process group with
   the real `hc_head` op, RMSNorm kernel, `ParallelLMHead` and `LogitsProcessor`, swept over draft
   batch. Four pairs per point, pair 0 discarded, arm order alternated.
4. **e2e, TP=2**: `vllm bench serve` on `DSV4-base-tpl`, fp8 KV cache, 1024 in / 512 out, 300
   prompts, `--max-concurrency 68`. Four interleaved pairs, pair 0 discarded.
5. **GSM8K A/B**: `lm_eval --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5`, greedy, all 1319 items,
   `enable_prefix_caching=False`, per-sample logging, **with a base-repeat control** (`base2`, a
   second run of the same build) so the noise floor is measured rather than assumed.

## Test Result

**Unit tests.** 3 passed. All 3 fail on the merge base. Dropping the shared-head RMSNorm fails 2 of
3; dropping `hc_head` fails 2 of 3. The norm gain is `normal_(1.0, 0.5)` and the `hc_head`
scale/base are non-trivial on purpose: an argmax is invariant to RMSNorm's per-row rescale, so a
default all-ones weight could not detect a skipped norm at all.

**Micro (TP=2).** This is a trade-off with a crossover, not a uniform win, so the crossover and the
absolute per-step cost matter more than any median over the sweep:

| shape | crossover (draft batch) | worst cost below | best saving above |
|---|---|---|---|
| hidden 4096, vocab 129280 | 36 → 44 | bs=6: +80.8 µs/step (−42.7 %) | bs=1028: −2496.6 µs/step (+80.1 %) |
| hidden 7168, vocab 129280 | 12 → 20 | bs=6: +29.6 µs/step (−12.4 %) | bs=1028: −2511.1 µs/step (+71.9 %) |

**Token agreement is 1.0000 at all 32 swept points**, on both the selected index and the selected
logit value. The crossover had to be recomputed for V4 rather than carried over from #56995's V3
numbers, and it differs between the two V4 shapes.

**e2e (TP=2, concurrency 68, above the crossover).** No change in either direction:

| metric | base | patched | pairwise median | pairwise range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total tok/s | 1935.13 | 1929.16 | −0.17 % | −0.92 … +1.26 % |
| Mean TPOT (ms) | 31.25 | 31.22 | +0.55 % | −0.73 … +0.62 % |
| Median TPOT (ms) | 30.37 | 30.48 | −0.07 % | −1.72 … +0.89 % |
| Mean TTFT (ms) | 584.73 | 588.33 | −1.11 % | −1.59 … −0.33 % |
| Acceptance length | 1.31 | 1.31 | −0.11 % | −1.08 … +0.67 % |

That is the expected result, and it is worth stating why rather than leaving it to be read as a
disappointment: the micro saving at the batch this run reached is 84.7 µs, while the measured
engine step is 40.83 ms (mean TPOT 31.25 ms × acceptance length 1.31), so the predicted e2e effect
is **+0.21 %** — an order of magnitude below the pair-to-pair spread. The e2e arm can show that
nothing regressed; it cannot resolve the win. Pair 0, had it been kept, would have read +8.41 %,
because the base arm alone rose from 1775.6 to 1935.1 tok/s between pair 0 and pair 1 on AITER JIT
warmup. Unchanged acceptance length is the e2e-level statement that the draft tokens did not
change.

**GSM8K (1319 items, 5-shot, greedy).**

| arm | strict | flexible |
|---|---|---|
| base | 0.9515 ± 0.0059 | 0.9507 ± 0.0060 |
| base2 (same build, control) | 0.9522 ± 0.0059 | 0.9530 ± 0.0058 |
| patched | 0.9500 ± 0.0060 | 0.9492 ± 0.0060 |

Effect (base → patched) is −0.0015 strict against a noise floor (base → base2) of +0.0008; both are
well inside the ±0.0059 stderr. Per-sample agreement is the sharper test and needs the same
control: base vs base2 produce identical text on **36.5 %** of items, base vs patched on **36.0 %**
— indistinguishable. Same-verdict rates are 98.1 % and 98.2 %. Two runs of one build already
disagree on most generations because vLLM's batching makes bf16 reductions batch-shape dependent,
so without the control column the 64 % of differing prompts would read as a regression. Claim: no
measurable accuracy change on GSM8K within the base-repeat noise floor — not bit-exactness.

**Not covered.** GSM8K exercises one shape of one path and says nothing about long context,
sampling or multi-turn.

---

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Model] Gemma4: register aliased embedding scalars as buffers
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose
`Gemma4Model` registers `normalizer` and the PLE scales (`embed_scale_per_layer`, `per_layer_input_scale`, `per_layer_projection_scale`) as non-persistent **buffers**, then passes them into the `@support_torch_compile` sub-wrapper `Gemma4SelfDecoderLayers`, which re-stored them as **plain tensor attributes**. `nn.Module._apply` (and thus `.to(device)`) only moves registered buffers/params, so on `model.to(<device>)` the parent's buffers move while the child's aliases stay on CPU — and the child is the module whose compiled `embed_input_ids` / `get_per_layer_inputs` / `project_per_layer_inputs` actually use them.

This is behaviorally invisible on CUDA (eager binary ops tolerate a 0-d CPU scalar via `TensorIterator::allow_cpu_scalars_`, and Inductor constant-folds it), so it produces correct results there. On a compiled backend with no notion of a live CPU graph input the compiled multiply fails to lower. gemma/gemma2/gemma3 are unaffected because they own the `normalizer` buffer in the same module that uses it.

## Fix
Register the four aliased scalars as non-persistent buffers in `Gemma4SelfDecoderLayers.__init__` so they follow the model on `.to(device)`. `register_buffer` accepts `None`, so the PLE-disabled case needs no branching. `persistent=False` matches the parent — these are config-derived constants, not checkpoint state, so `state_dict()` is unchanged. Embedding math is untouched; on CUDA this is behaviorally a no-op.

## Purpose

## Microbenchmarks

commits.pr_title: [CPU] Include vLLM Recipes tooling in release image to deploy models using vLLM Recipes
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Include the vLLM Recipes deployment tool in the official CPU serving image and document a one-step recipe-assisted serving workflow.

Previously, users of the pre-built CPU image needed a separate vLLM source checkout or had to generate `config.yml` and `env.sh` outside the container before using a vLLM Recipe.

This change copies `tools/recipes` into the CPU release image while keeping the existing `vllm serve` entrypoint unchanged. Users can opt into recipe-assisted serving with `serve_with_recipe.sh`.

A key benefit is that the tool queries https://recipes.vllm.ai/ at runtime. This allows users to combine an official vLLM CPU release image with the latest published recipe for their model and hardware, without rebuilding the image or manually copying recipe configuration files.

Example:

```bash
docker run --rm \
    --shm-size=4g \
    -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
    -p 8000:8000 \
    --env "HF_TOKEN=<secret>" \
    --entrypoint tools/recipes/serve_with_recipe.sh \
    vllm/vllm-openai-cpu:latest-x86_64 \
    --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
    --hardware xeon6
```

The workflow becomes:

`official CPU image` -> `latest published recipe` -> `hardware-aware configuration` -> `vllm serve`

The documentation is also updated to:
- show recipe-assisted serving from the pre-built CPU image;
- explain how to find the `--hardware` value from the vLLM Recipes hardware picker / URL;
- link the CPU supported-model recipe table to the one-step deployment flow; and
- keep the existing manual converter workflow available for users who want to inspect or customize generated configuration.

2. Verify `tools/recipes/serve_with_recipe.sh` is included in the release image.
3. Start a model using the recipe-assisted Docker workflow.
4. Verify the tool retrieves the selected recipe, detects Xeon hardware resources, generates `config.yml` and `env.sh`, and starts the vLLM OpenAI server.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Qwen4Exp] Release the profiling KV cache held by QSA key views
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Fixes #58960.

`QSAKeyStateCache.bind_kv_cache` stored the views `key_cache` and `rope_position_cache` next to `kv_cache`. `clear_layer_kv_caches` only resets `kv_cache`, so after CUDA graph memory profiling these views kept the profiling KV cache alive (9.76 GiB for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 at TP2) past `_teardown_profiling_state()`'s `empty_cache()`. It was freed only in the real `initialize_kv_cache`, stayed cached, and a later long-lived allocation pinned the block. FULL CUDA graph capture then ran out of memory at `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.90` with 9.38 GiB free but unreleasable in the default pool. The issue has the memory-snapshot evidence.

The change derives both views from `kv_cache` on access, so `kv_cache` is the only reference to the bound storage, the same contract Mamba layers follow. Read sites (`indexer_qsa.py` on NVIDIA and AMD) are unchanged; they get the same tensor views as before.

**Not a duplicate:** no open PR or issue covers QSA cache lifetime or profiling teardown for Qwen4Exp. #58439 and #58815 change Qwen4Exp PLE storage, not the QSA cache; #46515 fixes a different leak during CUDA graph memory profiling.

## Test Plan

```sh
# Regression test (new) and the rest of the QSA suite
pytest tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_qsa_reference.py -q

# End to end (2x RTX PRO 6000, TP2)
vllm serve nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 --language-model-only \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 --max-model-len 262144 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --reasoning-parser qwen3
```

## Test Result

- `test_clearing_qsa_key_cache_releases_its_storage` fails on `main` (the cleared layer still holds the bound storage) and passes with this change.
- `tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_qsa_reference.py`: 73 passed.
- `pre-commit` hooks (ruff-check, ruff-format, typos, mypy-3.10, check-test-tethering) pass on the changed files.
- End to end, same command, memory snapshots from the worker:

| default pool | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| free after KV cache init | 9.79 GiB (9,996 MiB profiling segment still held) | 0.02 GiB (segment released) |
| free before capture | 9.25 GiB, 9.23 GiB pinned in one segment | 3.95 GiB, largest segment 0.82 GiB and fully free |
| FULL CUDA graph capture | OOM in `qsa_select_paged_decode` | completes (`0.74 GiB (actual), 1.37 GiB (estimated)`), server ready |

Model evaluation: the change only affects when the profiling cache is freed; the views used at inference are the same tensors, so outputs are unchanged. For reference, the same model and stack at TP2 score 0.8931 on chat-template GSM8K (flexible-extract).

AI assistance was used (Claude) to investigate, write, and test this change.

commits.pr_title: [CPU] Use accelerator memory API in DiffusionGemma
commits.pr_body:
## Summary

Fix CPU execution in `DiffusionGemma` by using the supported PyTorch accelerator memory API when calculating the decode tile memory budget.

`current_platform.mem_get_info()` is not available on CPU, which caused inference to fail with:

```text
Current platform cpu does not have 'mem_get_info' attribute.
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
```

This change uses torch.accelerator.get_memory_info()[0], which is patched by the CPU backend to return NUMA-aware host memory information.

##  Validation

- python3 -m py_compile vllm/model_executor/models/diffusion_gemma.py
- git diff --check
- CPU container smoke test confirmed torch.accelerator.get_memory_info() returns valid free/total memory.
- End-to-end CPU serving test with google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it:
  - /health returned 200 OK
  - /v1/chat/completions returned 200 OK
  - Generated a 128-token response successfully
  - No mem_get_info, TypeError, Traceback, or ERROR appeared in server logs.

commits.pr_title: [Benchmark] Add Responses API backend to vllm bench serve
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

`vllm bench serve` cannot benchmark `/v1/responses`. `ASYNC_REQUEST_FUNCS` covers completions, chat, audio, embeddings, pooling and rerank, and there is an explicit `# TODO: Add more request functions for different API protocols.` right above it, but no Responses request function. This adds an `openai-responses` backend so the Responses protocol can be measured directly instead of routing the same workload through `/v1/chat/completions`.

The Responses stream is not shaped like the Chat Completions stream, so this is not the chat function with a different URL.

**Framing.** `_convert_stream_to_sse_events` emits `event: <type>\ndata: <json>\n\n`, so `message.removeprefix("data: ")` does not recover the payload. I added `_extract_sse_data` for the Responses path and left the Completions and Chat Completions loops untouched. It returns `None` for SSE comments, so the keep-alive comments added in #51034 are skipped rather than counted as tokens.

**TTFT.** Several events arrive before any token (`response.created`, `response.in_progress`, `response.output_item.added`, `response.content_part.added`). Only `response.output_text.delta` and `response.reasoning_text.delta` start the clock and contribute ITL. Reasoning deltas are included because the server is already decoding when it emits them, so excluding them would report an entire reasoning phase as time to first token.

**Generated text.** Only `response.output_text.delta` is accumulated. This is what `openai-chat` already does: the parser emits `DeltaMessage(reasoning=...)` with `content` unset, so a reasoning chunk sets TTFT and ITL but adds nothing to `generated_text`.

**E2EL and usage.** Latency stops at the last token event, so `latency - ttft` equals `sum(itl)` and TPOT is comparable with the other endpoints. This matches #55508, which fixed the same accounting on chat and audio. `input_tokens` / `output_tokens` come from the usage block on `response.completed`.

vLLM always ends a stream with `response.completed`, including on truncation, where it carries `status: "incomplete"`. The spec's `response.incomplete`, `response.failed` and `error` terminals are accepted too, since `vllm bench serve` can be pointed at other Responses servers, but vLLM does not emit them and the comments say so. Every event type string in the patch is one of the `Literal` values in `openai.types.responses`.

A stream that ends without any terminal event is failed rather than counted, so a proxy cutting the connection after a token cannot silently contribute a short E2EL and a missing usage block.

The payload sends `store: false`. It defaults to true, and a server started with `VLLM_ENABLE_RESPONSES_API_STORE=1` never evicts stored responses (`serving.py` says so in a FIXME), so a long run would grow the server heap.

One fix outside the request function: the `sonnet` dataset chose its prompt formatting by comparing the backend against `openai-chat`, so `openai-responses` received a client-side rendered chat template that the server then rendered a second time. It now takes the chat-style branch.

### OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_BACKENDS

Membership enables two things: `--ignore-eos` by default on random datasets, and the sampling parameter flags. I checked each against `ResponsesRequest`. `ignore_eos`, `temperature`, `top_p`, `top_k`, `frequency_penalty`, `presence_penalty` and `repetition_penalty` are all real fields. `min_p` is not, and `OpenAIBaseModel` sets `extra="allow"`, so the server would drop it with only a debug log. `bench serve` therefore rejects `--min-p` for this backend. A test validates the emitted payload against `ResponsesRequest` so this cannot drift silently.

### Out of scope

One streamed text generation request per prompt. No built-in tools, MCP, `previous_response_id`, background responses or tool call latency accounting. Multimodal datasets are already rejected for backends outside `multimodal_backends`.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest -v tests/benchmarks/test_responses_request_func.py
pre-commit run --files vllm/benchmarks/lib/endpoint_request_func.py vllm/benchmarks/serve.py tests/benchmarks/test_responses_request_func.py docs/benchmarking/cli.md
```

The tests drive the real request function against a local aiohttp server over a real socket, so the `event:` line, the token event types, the keep-alive comment and the usage block are all exercised end to end. They need no GPU and are picked up by the existing `Benchmarks CLI` step.

- **`test_openpangu_vl.py`, both cases.** #55941 fixed `OpenPanguVLForConditionalGeneration.get_input_embeddings` and added this test. #54142 was branched before #55941 and merged after it, and it brought back the old body with a `# type: ignore[call-overload]`. This PR puts #55941's `is_multimodal` mask back. mypy passes without the ignore. The model runner calls `embed_input_ids` rather than this method, so serving is unaffected, but anyone calling this public method directly gets the `TypeError`.
- **`test_mimo_v2_omni.py::test_window_attention_applies_sinks[2]`.** `vision_attn_env` was module-scoped. The autouse `cleanup_fixture` in `tests/conftest.py` tears down the TP group after every test, so the second parametrization always fails with `tensor model parallel group is not initialized`. commits.pr_title: [Perf][MRV2] Reuse Mamba/GDN metadata across KV cache groups
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

With #58207, `--min-kv-cache-group-layers` (default 3) trades KV capacity for fewer KV cache groups, because every group rebuilds its attention metadata each step. For Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash that's 17 groups instead of 46 and 30% less KV cache (RFC #58638, question 1). GDN groups with the same spec differ only in their state indices. This builds the first group's metadata and derives the others with `update_block_table()`, also at capture, so later groups' FULL graphs read the first group's batch-level buffers.

- `build_attn_metadata` does this for groups with the same `MambaSpec` and builder type, if the builder supports `update_block_table()`. No GDN-specific code in the runner.
- GDN implements `update_block_table()` and takes MRV2's precomputed `mamba_aligned_state_indices`.
- Mamba1/2 builders already support `update_block_table()` without spec decoding, so their metadata is now reused too.

Opened as part of [model runner discussion](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52297#discussion_r4089381401) on #52297. Implements @MarkXCloud's second suggestion there. Same idea as #35166 by @jennyyyyzhen, which was closed as stale.
@xyang16 explicitly added as co author, since the original idea developed in their PR

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest tests/v1/attention/test_gdn_metadata_builder.py tests/models/kimi_k3/test_kda_metadata.py tests/v1/worker/test_mamba_hybrid_model_state.py
```

commits.pr_title: [Model] Enable LoRA support for RobertaForSequenceClassification
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Enable LoRA adapter serving for `RobertaForSequenceClassification` (and its
registry alias `XLMRobertaForSequenceClassification`).

These models are widely used as cross-encoder rerankers (e.g.
`cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`, `BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3`). Adding
LoRA support allows serving a single base model with multiple fine-tuned
adapters via `LoRARequest`, avoiding the need to merge and redeploy full model
copies for each adapter.

The change follows the same pattern as ModernBertModel (#57148):
- Add `SupportsLoRA` to the class bases
- Declare `packed_modules_mapping` for the fused `qkv_proj` layer

The underlying `BertModel` already uses `QKVParallelLinear` for the fused
QKV projection, which is LoRA-compatible. The component names (`query`, `key`,
`value`) match the HuggingFace weight names that PEFT adapters target.

## Test Plan

Tested with a PEFT LoRA adapter (rank 256) trained on
`cross-encoder/mmarco-mMiniLMv2-L12-H384-v1` (RoBERTa-based cross-encoder)
using vLLM's `LLM.score()` API with `LoRARequest`. Verified:
- Engine starts with `enable_lora=True` without errors
- Adapter loads and produces scores
- Scores are numerically equivalent to the merge-and-unload approach
  (max absolute difference < 0.01, cosine similarity > 0.999)

Benchmark on L4 GPU (bf16, eager mode, max_lora_rank=256):
- Base model: p50=76ms, ~422 pairs/s

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Frontend] Use a fresh parser per choice in non-streaming chat completions
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

**Bug:** non-streaming `/v1/chat/completions` with `n > 1` parses every choice with the *same* parser instance, so parser state from one choice leaks into the next. Streaming already uses one parser per choice.

**Visible symptom:** Kimi K2-style tool-call IDs (`functions.<name>:<idx>`) keep counting across choices. With `n=2` and one tool call per choice, non-streaming returns `get_weather:0` and `get_weather:1`, while streaming returns `get_weather:0` for both. With H prior tool calls in the history, non-streaming gives `:H`, `:H+1`; streaming gives `:H` for each.

**Fix:** `chat_completion_full_generator` keeps the existing parser for choice 0 and builds a fresh one for each later choice (`n=1` creates no extra parser). The constructor call moves into a small `_make_parser` helper shared with the streaming path, which is otherwise unchanged. No protocol change: non-streaming now matches streaming.

## Test Plan

Live server A/B on one H200: the same requests against the parent commit `e7900156e1` (before) and this branch (after).

```bash
VLLM_ENFORCE_STRICT_TOOL_CALLING=0 vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --max-model-len 4096 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser hermes \
  --hf-overrides '{"model_type": "kimi_k2"}'
```

`--hf-overrides` makes a small model use Kimi K2 tool-call IDs, and `VLLM_ENFORCE_STRICT_TOOL_CALLING=0` routes `required`/named `tool_choice` through the parser path that assigns them.

Example request (other cases vary `messages`, `tool_choice`, `n`, `stream`):

```bash
curl -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", "n": 2, "temperature": 0.8, "seed": 7, "max_tokens": 128,
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in Tokyo?"}],
  "tools": [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_weather",
    "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["city"]}}}],
  "tool_choice": "required",
  "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}
}' | jq '[.choices[].message.tool_calls[0].id]'
```

## Test Result

Tool-call IDs per choice (`functions.get_weather:<idx>`):

| Request | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| non-streaming, `n=2`, `tool_choice=required` | `:0`, `:1` ❌ | `:0`, `:0` |
| non-streaming, `n=2`, `required`, 2 prior tool calls in history | `:2`, `:3` ❌ | `:2`, `:2` |
| non-streaming, `n=2`, named `tool_choice` | `:0`, `:1` ❌ | `:0`, `:0` |
| non-streaming, `n=1`, `required` | `:0` | `:0` |
| streaming, `n=2`, `required` (reference) | `:0`, `:0` | `:0`, `:0` |
| streaming, `n=2`, `required`, with history (reference) | `:2`, `:2` | `:2`, `:2` |

Also sent `n=2` with `tool_choice=auto` (Hermes random IDs), plain `n=2` chat, and `n=3` with thinking enabled. With IDs removed, the before/after responses for all nine requests are identical: the only change is the three non-streaming ID fixes above.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Frontend] Sample batched chat completions from the adjusted requests
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Fixes #42103. Supersedes #42105.

`/v1/chat/completions/batch` created every per-conversation `ChatCompletionRequest` twice. The renderer ran the parser's `adjust_request` on the first copy, then the endpoint sampled from the second, unadjusted copy. Parser adjustments therefore never reached `SamplingParams` in batch mode. These include `skip_special_tokens=False`, the Mistral grammar and structural tags. With a reasoning parser such as Gemma 4, the engine strips the `<channel|>` end marker. Reasoning then never ends: the answer is absorbed into `reasoning` and `content` comes back `null`.

`render_batch_chat_request` now returns the requests it rendered, and `create_batch_chat_completion` samples from those. This matches the non-batch path. The batch-level parser is now built after rendering, so it reads `chat_template_kwargs` from the adjusted request. Non-batch chat is unchanged.

This PR supersedes #42105 (@Kimahriman). That PR takes the same approach but has had merge conflicts since May, targets APIs that no longer exist, and also changes `reasoning_ended` handling. This PR keeps only the request fix, rebased on current `main`.

## Test Plan

**Setup:** A/B on one H200, same GPU and port, one server at a time. Model `google/gemma-4-E4B-it`, `temperature=0`, `seed=1234`, `chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": true}`. The "before" server ran from a `main` checkout, the "after" server from this branch. Server command (identical for both):

```bash
python -m vllm.entrypoints.cli.main serve google/gemma-4-E4B-it --port 8011 \
  --reasoning-parser gemma4 --enable-log-requests --max-model-len 8192
```

Batch request with two conversations: `"What is 17 * 23? Give just the number."` and `"Which is larger, 9.11 or 9.9? Answer in one word."`.

**Before (`main`):** batch choice 1 has the answer stuck inside `reasoning`, and `content` is `null`.

```json
{
  "index": 1,
  "reasoning": "...I will provide the number as the single-word answer.9.9",
  "content": null
}
```

```text
Received request chatcmpl-882284ede918a9ef_0: params: SamplingParams(... skip_special_tokens=True ...)
Received request chatcmpl-882284ede918a9ef_1: params: SamplingParams(... skip_special_tokens=True ...)
```

**After (this PR):** reasoning ends cleanly and the answer is in `content`.

```json
{
  "index": 1,
  "reasoning": "...I will provide the number as the single-word answer.",
  "content": "9.9"
}
```

```text
Received request chatcmpl-ad0dc647e98ebeca_0: params: SamplingParams(... skip_special_tokens=False ...)
Received request chatcmpl-ad0dc647e98ebeca_1: params: SamplingParams(... skip_special_tokens=False ...)
```

**Full comparison:**

| Check | Before (`main`) | After (this PR) |
|---|---|---|
| Batch, thinking on, choice 1 | `content: null`, answer inside `reasoning` | `content: "9.9"`, clean `reasoning` |
| Batch sub-request `skip_special_tokens` | `True` (non-batch sends `False`) | `False`, matches non-batch |
| Non-batch `/v1/chat/completions`, thinking on (control) | `"391"` | identical |
| Batch, thinking off | `"391"` / `"9.9"` | identical |
| Batch, `response_format` json_schema | `{"answer": "yes"}` / `{"answer": "no"}` | identical |

Choice 0 (`"391"`) has no reasoning on either side because the model skips thinking for that prompt, including non-batch.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Frontend] Count Responses reasoning tokens per tool round
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

With `VLLM_USE_EXPERIMENTAL_PARSER_CONTEXT=1`, a Responses request that makes tool calls underreports `usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`: it counts only the first round's reasoning.

`ParsableContext` never counted reasoning tokens, so `responses_full_generator` counted the output ids of all rounds concatenated, in one parser pass. For templates that put `<think>\n` in the generation prompt (Qwen3, Qwen3.5), later rounds have no generated opener, so their reasoning follows round 1's `</think>` and is counted as content.

This PR counts each round on its own ids in `ParsableContext.append_output`, and limits the serving fallback to `SimpleContext`.

## Test Plan

Same GPU, same request, baseline `main` (924707f1bf) vs this PR, temperature 0.

```bash
VLLM_USE_EXPERIMENTAL_PARSER_CONTEXT=1 \
PYTHON_EXECUTION_BACKEND=dangerously_use_uv \
VLLM_ENABLE_RESPONSES_API_STORE=1 \
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B \
    --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
    --enable-auto-tool-choice \
    --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder \
    --tool-server demo \
    --max-model-len 16384
```

Request: "What is 123 * 456? Use python to calculate the result." with `tools=[{"type": "code_interpreter", "container": {"type": "auto"}}]`. This path does not render `code_interpreter` into the prompt (the same reason `test_mcp_tool_call` is xfailed), so its schema is described in `instructions`. The model calls it once, the demo python tool returns `56088`, and the model answers in a second round.

Expected `reasoning_tokens` = tokenized length of each `reasoning` output item, summed: **34 + 35 = 69**.

**Before (`main`)**: only round 1 is counted

```text
reasoning   "The user wants me to calculate 123 * 456 using Python ..."        34 tokens
mcp_call    code_interpreter  "result = 123 * 456; print(result)"  ->  56088
reasoning   "The Python code successfully calculated 123 * 456 = 56088 ..."   35 tokens
message     "The result of 123 * 456 is **56088**."

usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens = 34   ✗
```

**After (this PR)**: both rounds are counted

```text

reasoning   "The Python code successfully calculated 123 * 456 = 56088 ..."   35 tokens
```

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][KV Connector] Retry Mooncake bootstrap registration on timeout (reopens #55763)
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Fixes #55729.

This PR reopens #55763 and credit goes to @Sarimsaljook, the original PR author. Compared with #55763, the attempt limit is now an internal constant set to 3 instead of a user-facing environment variable. The original tests and documentation are adapted accordingly; the remaining fix is preserved.

During slow rank-0 initialization, bootstrap registration can time out. Previously, only connection errors were retried, and a failed sender listener could leave startup waiting indefinitely.

This change:

- Adds an explicit registration timeout through `VLLM_MOONCAKE_CONNECTOR_TIMEOUT` (default: 30 seconds).
- Retries connection errors and timeouts for up to 3 total attempts, with exponential backoff.
- Makes repeated registration of the same worker address idempotent, while still rejecting conflicting addresses.
- Bounds the sender-listener readiness wait and propagates startup failures.

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][Bugfix] Fall back to default GEMM for CPU tensors on ROCm builds
commits.pr_body:
## Why this is not duplicating an existing PR

Searched for existing fixes before starting: `gh pr list --search "rocm_unquantized_gemm"`, `--search "test_gemma.py"`, `--search "gemma4_dspark"`, and the ~20 open/merged DSpark/confidence-head PRs in this area — none touch `dispatch_unquantized_gemm`/`rocm_unquantized_gemm` or this device-dispatch bug. Filed as vllm-project/vllm#58922 for tracking.

## What broke

`tests/models/language/generation/test_gemma.py::test_gemma4_dspark_loads_confidence_head` (added in #57263, merged 2026-09-26) fails on ROCm CI:

```
NotImplementedError: Could not run 'vllm::rocm_unquantized_gemm' with arguments
from the 'CPU' backend. ... 'vllm::rocm_unquantized_gemm' is only available for
these backends: [CUDA, ...]
```

`dispatch_unquantized_gemm()` picks `rocm_unquantized_gemm` for any ROCm build purely from `current_platform.is_rocm()`, ignoring the tensor's actual device. The custom op is only registered for the CUDA/HIP dispatch key, so a CPU tensor (as this test uses, exercising `DSparkConfidenceHead.proj`, a `ReplicatedLinear`, without moving it to a GPU) hard-crashes. The CUDA and CPU branches of the same dispatcher already fall back to plain `torch.nn.functional.linear` for this kind of case; the ROCm branch didn't.

This surfaced while running full ROCm CI on an unrelated PR (#58867, AITER version bump) — `amd-mi355-dpx-language-models-extended-generation` is `optional: true` and never ran on #57263 itself, so it was never caught.

## Fix

Add the same device fallback the CUDA/CPU branches already have:

```python
def rocm_unquantized_gemm(layer, x, weight, bias=None):
    if not x.is_cuda:
        return default_unquantized_gemm(layer, x, weight, bias)
    return torch.ops.vllm.rocm_unquantized_gemm(x, weight, bias)
```

No change to real GPU-tensor behavior/perf; only changes the previously-crashing CPU-tensor case.

## Test commands run and results

Could not run pytest locally (this sandbox has no torch/GPU install); relying on ROCm CI (`amd-mi355-dpx-language-models-extended-generation`) to validate `test_gemma4_dspark_loads_confidence_head` now passes, and the rest of the ROCm suite to confirm no regression from the added device check.

## AI assistance disclosure

This fix was investigated and written with AI assistance (Cursor agent) while triaging CI failures on #58867; I reviewed the change and root-cause analysis before opening this PR.

commits.pr_title: [Perf][MoE] Use fused MiniMax2 routing with non-unit routed scaling
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

`get_routing_method_type` maps sigmoid + correction bias + renormalize routing (no expert groups) to `RoutingMethodType.MiniMax2` only when `routed_scaling_factor` is 1.0 (added in #44347). MiniMax-M3 uses `routed_scaling_factor=2.0`, so its MoE falls back to `Unspecified`. On SM100 with the MXFP8 checkpoint, that means the modular TRT-LLM path: a separate vLLM `topk_sigmoid` launch per MoE layer, then `trtllm_fp8_block_scale_routed_moe`.

The restriction is no longer needed with the pinned FlashInfer 0.7.0:
- FlashInfer's MiniMax2 routing uses `routed_scaling_factor` as its route scale: final weight = `sigmoid(x) * routeScale / sum` (`trtllm_fused_moe_routing_runner.cu`: `routingData.mRouteScale = routedScalingFactor`).
- Every monolithic TRT-LLM caller that accepts MiniMax2 already passes `routed_scaling_factor` through: FP8 block scale / MXFP8, FP8 per-tensor, and NVFP4.
- The scale is not applied twice. When `apply_routed_scale_to_output` is false, which is the M3 case, the scale goes to the router and the runner gets 1.0.

This PR removes the restriction, and with it the now-unused `routed_scaling_factor` argument of `get_routing_method_type`.

The restriction also, by accident, kept zero-expert models (`ZeroExpertRouter`) off kernels with built-in routing whenever their scale was not 1.0. Those kernels cannot reproduce zero-expert handling, and with scale 1.0 such a model was already mapped to MiniMax2. `ZeroExpertRouter.routing_method_type` now returns `Unspecified` explicitly.

Effect: any model with sigmoid + bias + renormalize routing, no expert groups, and a non-unit scale becomes eligible for the monolithic TRT-LLM kernels on Blackwell. MiniMax-M3 is one such model. The routing semantics are the same as vLLM's `fused_topk_bias`: biased scores select the experts, unbiased sigmoid gives the weights, which are renormalized and scaled.

**Not a duplicate:** I searched open PRs for `MiniMax2 routed_scaling_factor`, `MiniMax-M3 routing trtllm`, `minimax m3 moe routing fused` and `RoutingMethodType MiniMax2`. Nothing touches this mapping. The related merged PRs are #39141 and #44347, and #44347 introduced the restriction.

## Test Plan

```bash
# Routing-method unit tests (new: MiniMax2 with scale 2.0, zero-expert -> Unspecified)
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_routing.py -k "routing or degenerate or grouped or zero or minimax"
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_topk_softplus_sqrt.py -k routing_method

# New GPU test (SM100): monolithic MXFP8 TRT-LLM with fused MiniMax2 routing and
# routed_scaling_factor=2.0 vs modular TRT-LLM with vLLM fused_topk_bias routing
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_flashinfer.py -k "minimax2_routing or deferred_finalize"

# End to end, MiniMax-M3-MXFP8, TP4 on 4x GB300, this branch vs main
vllm serve MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 -tp 4 --max-model-len 8192
python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --num-questions 1319 --max-concurrency 64
vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 256 \
    --ignore-eos --max-concurrency {1,8} --num-prompts {16,128}
```

## Test Result

**Unit tests:**
- `test_routing.py`: 507 passed.
- The routing-method test in `test_topk_softplus_sqrt.py` passed.
- `test_flashinfer.py -k "minimax2_routing or deferred_finalize"`: 6 passed on GB300.
- Both new routing tests fail without the source change.
- The new FlashInfer test fails if the fused path ignores the scale: about 80% of elements mismatch, with a max abs diff of 0.39.
- pre-commit passes.

**Backend actually selected** (server log, MiniMax-M3-MXFP8):
- main: `Using MoEPrepareAndFinalizeNoDPEPModular`
- this PR: `Using MoEPrepareAndFinalizeNoDPEPMonolithic`

**Kernel level** (GB300, M3 MoE shapes: H=6144, 128 experts, top-4, MXFP8, 57 MoE layers captured in one CUDA graph; µs per layer):

| tokens | TP4 (I=768): separate top-k | TP4: fused | TP1 (I=3072): separate top-k | TP1: fused |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 17.00 | 15.40 | 48.06 | 46.11 |
| 4 | 44.92 | 42.91 | 118.65 | 117.33 |
| 16 | 88.79 | 86.97 | 271.33 | 269.70 |
| 32 | 115.48 | 113.79 | 408.86 | 406.99 |
| 64 | 146.34 | 146.31 | 548.63 | 546.83 |
| 256 | 219.59 | 219.56 | 852.83 | 851.90 |

Fusing the routing saves about 1.3–2 µs per MoE layer at decode batch sizes. At TP4 that is 91–115 µs per decode step for ≤32 tokens, and about 9% of the MoE time at batch 1. The max relative difference between the two outputs is 4–6e-3.

**End to end, MiniMax-M3-MXFP8, TP4, 4x GB300:**

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| TPOT, concurrency 1 | 4.14 ms | 3.96 ms (-4.3%) |
| Output throughput, concurrency 1 | 233.0 tok/s | 243.5 tok/s (+4.5%) |
| TPOT, concurrency 8 | 7.37 ms | 7.18 ms (-2.6%) |
| Output throughput, concurrency 8 | 942.9 tok/s | 966.2 tok/s (+2.5%) |
| GSM8K, 5-shot, 1319 questions | 0.861 / 0.851 / 0.862 / 0.847 (mean 0.855) | 0.853 / 0.861 / 0.852 / 0.860 (mean 0.857) |

The eval is greedy, and each version was run 4 times (4 separate runs, 2 server launches). The spread comes from batch nondeterminism: 1.5 points on main, 0.9 points with this PR. The means match.

**AI assistance:** Claude Code was used for the investigation, the implementation, the tests and the benchmarks. All results above come from runs on 4x GB300.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Support repsonse_format + tool_choice=auto
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Fixes https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/39929

In case request has both response_format and tool_choice=auto then we construct structural tags for both constraints and do OR of them.

**IMPORTANT:** to construct structural tag for tools we do a simple trick. Since tool_choice=auto allows by default a tool call or any text, then we cannot use that structural tag. Instead we create a structural tag manually specifying tool_choice to be set as `required`. In that case structural tag would not allow arbitrary text but only valid tool call.

Some time ago there was added support for response_format + tool_choice=required case: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32127
But the idea of this PR #32127 was a bit different and simplier to drop response_format from request and allow only tool call. Current PR #56086 saves both constraints, so the logic behind this patch is a little bit more complicated.

Previous attempts to fix this bug:
* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/39969
* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47439
* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47394

All these PRs were closed for unknown reasons, I added authors of these PRs to co-authors.

commits.pr_title: [Perf][Pooling] Avoid blocking seq_lens GPU-to-CPU copy for pooling in FlashInfer metadata builder
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose
FlashInfer's metadata builder needs per-request sequence lengths on the CPU to plan paged KV metadata. For V2 model runner, `seq_lens` live on the GPU, so the builder fetches them with `common_attn_metadata.seq_lens.cpu()`. For pooling models this copy is avoidable; pooling models have no speculative tokens, so `seq_lens_cpu_upper_bound` maintained by the model runner is exact, not optimistic. The pooling runner already relies on this (`pooling_runner.py`: ["Pooling has no speculative tokens, so this CPU upper bound is exact"](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.29.0/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pool/pooling_runner.py#L142)). 

This results in a measured performance boost of about 1.35%.
